## Concurrency in C#

Use **`Task`** and **`Task.Run`** for parallel CPU work, **`async`/`await`** for asynchronous workflows, and **`System.Threading.Channels.Channel`** for producer/consumer queues that feel similar to Go channels or Rust `mpsc`.

Prefer **`CancellationToken`** in real services; these exercises keep output deterministic without wall-clock races.

exercises.title: Spawn thread
exercises.description: Run work on a background thread, wait ~100ms on the main thread, then join so `Hello!` always appears before `main done`.
hints: `Task.Run` schedules a delegate on the thread pool

exercises.title: Channel
exercises.description: Use an unbounded **`Channel<string>`**: a worker writes `ping`; main reads and prints it (with newline).

exercises.title: Bounded channel
exercises.description: Create a **bounded** channel with capacity `2`, send `10` then `20`, and print both values separated by a space (no trailing newline).
hints: Use `Console.Write` for the space-separated layout without a trailing newline

exercises.title: First ready
exercises.description: Spawn a thread that sleeps 10ms then sends `from ch1` through a channel; main receives and prints that string.
hints: `Console.Write` avoids an extra newline when the expected line has none

exercises.title: Close / drain
exercises.description: Producer sends `1`, `2`, `3` then completes the channel; consumer prints each line until reads fail.

exercises.title: Fan-in
exercises.description: Two workers enqueue `hello` and `world`; collect both strings, sort, and print one per line.
hints: Join both tasks before sorting for deterministic collection

exercises.title: Join handles
exercises.description: Print `1`, `2`, `3` on separate lines by running three tasks **sequentially** (each finishes before the next starts), then print `done`.
